Section 226, read with  section 205, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection and recovery of tax - Other modes of recovery - Assessment year 1986-87 - Person responsible for deducting tax at source from lottery prize, after having deducted tax at source from prize amounts of lottery payable to assessee, failed to deposit money so deducted in Government treasury - Assessing Officer thereafter issued notices under section 226(3) to assessee's bankers to satisfy tax liability from his bank account - Single Judge set aside ITO's order holding it to be contrary to provisions of section 205 - Whether deduction of tax being only one of modes of recovery of tax and once this mode is adopted and by virtue of statutory provision person responsible for deducting tax at source deducted the amount, only that mode should be pursued for purposes of recovery of tax liability without subjecting assessee to other modes of recovery of tax by recovering amount once again to satisfy tax liability - Held, yes - Whether where person responsible for TDS deducted amount and failed to deposit it in Government treasury, he should be deemed to be an assessee-in-default under section 201, and whatever process or coercive measures are permissible under law can only be taken against such person and not assessee - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, recovery of such tax by issuing notice to assessee's bankers was illegal - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee won two lottery prizes during the period relevant to the assessment year 1986-87. The agency, while making payment of prize money to the assessee, deducted the tax at source but did not deposit the money so deducted in the Government treasury. According to the agency, in absence of relevant records having been forwarded to the Chairman, Vaibhavshali Bumper, they were not able to furnish the date of payment of taxes to the treasury. The Assessing Officer rejected the agency's explanation and, while making assessment, did not give credit for the TDS to the assessee but observed that the credit for this would be given only when evidence as to actual payment of the same was produced.

The Assessing Officer issued two notices under section 226(3) to the assessee's bankers directing them to pay the dues forthwith, failing which usual consequences under different sections of the Act would follow.

On writ, the assessee impugned the orders/notices of attachment and prayed for a direction to the Assessing Officer to give credit for TDS The Single Judge set aside the impugned order holding it to be contrary to the provisions of section 205.

On appeal :

HELD: On facts, it appeared to be a case where, in all probability, the amount was deducted at source by the agency from the prize money payable to the assessee but the same did not seem to have been made over to the Government treasury for payment to the Central Government.

A certificate of deduction is to be provided by the person deducting the tax as provided under section 203. There is a bar against direct demand on the assessee where the tax is deducted at source as provided under section 205. The assessee is not supposed to do any thing in the whole transaction except that he has to accept the payment of the reduced amount from which is deducted income-tax at source. The responsibility to deposit the amount deducted at source as tax is that of the person who is responsible to deduct the tax at source. On the amount being deducted, the assessee only gets a certificate to that effect by the person responsible to deduct the tax. In a case where the amount has been deducted by the person responsible to deduct the amount under the statutory provisions, the assessee has no control over the matter. In case of default in making over the amount to the account of the Central Government, it is obviously the person responsible to deduct or the person who has made the deduction who is held responsible for the same. The responsibility of such person is to the extent that he has to be deemed to be an assessee-in-default in respect of the tax.

HEADNOTE: Section 205, read with sections 192, 199 and 203, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection and recovery of tax - Bar against direct demand on assessee - Assessment year 1996-97 - Whether in view of section 205, income-tax authorities, under no circumstances, can make assessee liable to make payment of any tax to extent to which tax has been deducted at source by person paying salary to assessee under section 192 - Held, yes - Whether, however, at same time, credit for tax deducted at source cannot be given to assessee unless he submits certificate as prescribed under section 203 in 
 respect of TDS as per provisions of section 199 - Held, yes - Whether till powers available to income-tax authorities to enforce payment of tax by deductor and also enforce issue of certificate in respect thereof to payee were not exercised by revenue authorities to corner deductor of tax, no tax as well as interest pertaining thereto could be recovered from assessee - Held, yes.

FACT: The assessee’s employer paid salary to him after deducting the tax therefrom. But despite repeated requests made by the assessee, his employer did not furnish the requisite TDS certificate. Consequently, he filed his return without Form No. 16 and also requested the Assessing Officer to enforce the issue of said certificate by the employer in exercise of his jurisdiction over the matter. However, in the absence of the same, the Assessing Officer framed the assessment under section 143(1)(a) raising tax demand in respect of salary income which was levied for the TDS certificate not furnished as well as interest payable in respect of the said tax. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that in the absence of Form No. 16 and Form No. 24, giving credit for TDS on salary did not appear to be justified, though the assessee could not be asked to pay the tax again to the extent to which tax had already been deducted in view of section 205. He, accordingly, directed the Assessing Officer to ask the assessee to obtain the same from the employer and furnish the same.

On second appeal :

HELD: Tax had been deducted from the salary of the assessee by the employer. In this view of the factual position, section 205 really put a bar against direct demand on the assessee. The interest leviable in respect of TDS also is a consequence of non-furnishing of certificate by the assessee in respect of TDS. Had the employer given the assessee a TDS certificate, no interest could be levied on the assessee as the same was to be reduced while computing assessed tax. However, at the same time, credit for tax deducted at source cannot be given to an assessee unless the assessee submits certificate as prescribed under section 203 in respect of TDS as per provisions of section 199. [Para 5]

Hence, in view of section 205, the authorities under no circumstances could make the assessee liable to make payment of any tax to the extent to which the tax had been deducted at source by the person paying the salary to the assessee under section 192. However, as TDS certificate had not been given by deductor, the credit of TDS could not be given. Under the peculiar circumstances of the case, the income-tax authorities were directed not to recover any tax levied on the assessee in respect of non-furnishing of TDS certificate. There are various provisions in the Act which provide the powers to the income-tax authorities to enforce the payment of tax by deductor and also enforce issue of certificate in respect thereof to the payee. There was no material on record to show that whether such powers had been exercised by the department to enforce the payment of tax deducted at source and also for the issue of certificate thereof. In that view of the situation, the assessee could not be held liable for the consequences which were beyond the control of the assessee, i.e., non-furnishing of TDS certificate. Till such powers were not exercised by the revenue authorities to corner the deductor of tax, i.e., to collect payment of TDS from him and also to obtain the certificate, no tax as well as interest pertaining thereto could be recovered from the assessee. The appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed in the aforesaid terms. [Para 6]

The said order was necessary so that further consequences could follow and the assessee could file an appeal against the specific order by the Assessing Officer. [Para 18]

On that account alone, the order of the Assessing Officer under section 201(1) was liable to be quashed. [Para 19] In the instant case, the Assessing Officer had not levied any penalty under section 221. He had only directed to recover the deficiency of tax deducted at source. In addition, interest under section 201(1A) was levied. Coming to the merits of the case, it was clear that the assessment of the employees to whom conveyance allowance was paid, must have been completed before the date when order under sections 201(1) and 201(1A) was passed. The shortfall in tax, if any, in the deduction of tax at source had to be paid back by the employees while filing their returns. Section 140A has been enacted to meet out the contingency where tax deducted at source and advance tax, etc., is less than tax as per return of income. If on assessment of an employee under section 143(3), further demand is raised, then that demand could be recovered from the employee. There is no provision in the Act which empowers the Assessing Officer to raise the demand in the hands of the employee and simultaneously also raise the demand against the employer on account of short deduction or non-deduction. It could have been a separate and different case had the Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 221 after declaring the assessee as deemed to be in default. But in the instant case, the deficient demand for TDS could not be raised against the employer-assessee after the completion of assessment of the employees. The mechanism to give credit of deficient tax as per section 201(1) collected after the completion of assessment of the concerned employees would fail as no such credit could be given. That would create an unjust enrichment of the revenue, which is not permissible. Thus, the Assessing Officer was incorrect in directing to recover the deficient tax from the employer after the expiry of limitation of completion of assessment of the employees. [Para 20]

There is another aspect of the problem where tax deducted or short deducted has not been actually paid. The machinery for computing interest under section 201(1A) will fail. Where deficient tax has not been paid, there will not be an outer limit of time for computation of interest. The interest as per section 201(1A) is chargeable from the date on which such tax (deficient tax) was deductible ending on the date on which such tax was actually paid. Thus, where deficient tax has not been paid, interest cannot run in perpetuity. In the instant case also, the alleged deficient tax had not been paid. Hence, interest under section 201(1A) could not be charged from the employer-assessee. [Para 23]

In view of the above, the employer-assessee could not be faulted for holding an honest opinion that conveyance allowance was not to be included in the computation of income of employees while deducting tax at source. Hence, he could not be declared as an assessee deemed to be in default. Therefore, interest under section 201(1A) could not be charged from him. [Para 25]

In the result, the appeals of the assessee were allowed and that of the revenue dismissed.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The admission of additional evidence in appellate proceedings is governed by rule 29 of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal Rules, 1963. Courts have consistently emphasised that the admission of such evidence should align with the principles of natural justice, particularly when it is crucial for the fair adjudication of a dispute. [Para 6.1]

■ The additional evidence directly addresses the Commissioner (Appeals) observations regarding non-compliance with procedural requirements under rule 37BA. It demonstrates that the assessee had taken proactive steps to ensure the transfer of TDS credit but faced procedural delays beyond its control. The evidence is crucial in establishing the bona fide actions of the assessee and directly impacts the determination of TDS credit entitlement, which is central to the appeal. The evidence submitted goes to the root of the matter, clarifying that the assessee was not negligent or non-compliant but was actively pursuing the transfer of TDS credit. This information was not furnished earlier due to the assessee's belief that, since the income was correctly offered to tax, the TDS credit would naturally follow. The documents are relevant as they demonstrate the procedural compliance required by rule 37BA and counter the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the assessee failed to take appropriate actions. [Para 6.2]

■

The denial of TDS credit to the assessee hinges primarily on procedural lapses, specifically the non-reflection of TDS credit in Form 26AS and the failure to comply with rule 37BA. However, a critical aspect that needs to be addressed is the role of third parties—namely Citibank NA and CS - in causing these procedural lapses. Citibank, acting as the depository for V ADRs, withheld tax at source when the ADRs were compulsorily redeemed. Due to the absence of the assessee’s PAN at the time of deduction, the TDS credit was incorrectly attributed under the category 'without PAN' or in the name of the broker, CS rather than the assessee, Testec Asia Limited. This misattribution led to the TDS credit not reflecting in the assessee’s Form 26AS, which is a procedural issue outside the control of the assessee. Upon obtaining a PAN, the assessee actively engaged with Citibank and CS to correct the TDS attribution. The assessee submitted its PAN and requested that the credit be transferred correctly to its account. Despite continuous communication and submission of necessary documents, including confirmations, these procedural corrections were not completed in time to reflect in the assessee’s Form 26AS at the stage of assessment, highlighting that the delay was not due to any lack of effort on the assessee’s part. [Para 6.5]

■

It is a well-established principle of natural justice that a taxpayer should not suffer due to procedural lapses caused by third parties, especially when the taxpayer has acted in good faith and made all reasonable efforts to rectify the situation. It is consistently held on many judicial forums that the substance of compliance—namely, offering income to tax—should take precedence over procedural errors when assessing a taxpayer’s entitlement to TDS credit. Section 205 protects the taxpayer from being asked to pay tax again if tax has already been deducted at source. This principle supports the argument that TDS credit, once deducted, should not be denied based on procedural failures, particularly those not attributable to the taxpayer. Rule 37BA provides for the mechanism of TDS credit, intending to ensure that the credit is given to the person who offers the income for taxation. The primary objective of this rule is to align TDS credit with the person who is the beneficial owner of the income. In this case, the assessee is the rightful owner of the income from Vedanta ADRs, and despite procedural errors by Citibank, the assessee has fulfilled the substantive requirements by declaring the income in its tax return. Denying credit due to procedural lapses by third parties contradicts the rule’s purpose. From revenue perspective, allowing TDS credit to the assessee where the corresponding income has been offered does not result in any revenue loss to the exchequer. The tax has been deducted and accounted for; it is merely the credit that has been procedurally misplaced due to third-party errors. [Para 6.6]

■

In light of the above, the denial of TDS credit based solely on procedural grounds is not justified. The assessee is entitled to the TDS credit as claimed. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is set aside. The Assessing Officer is directed to grant the TDS credit accordingly and adjust the same against the tax demand raised. [Para 6.7]

HEADNOTE: Section  199,  read with section  143,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  390,  read with section  270  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Deduction of tax at source – Credit for tax deducted (Illustrations) - Assessment year  2019-20  - Assessee filed return declaring total income of about Rs. 33.96 lakhs - On processing return under section 143(1), CPC raised demand of about Rs. 4.27 lakhs after allowing matched TDS credit of about Rs. 6.02 lakhs and treating balance TDS claim of about Rs. 3.65 lakhs as mismatched - CIT(A) upheld denial of TDS credit holding that credit under section 199 read with Rule 37BA is allowable on basis of Form 26AS/TDS certificates - Whether since assessee, on basis of synopsis and paper book, demonstrated full payment of TDS by deductor in favour of deductee assessee, impugned order deserved to be set aside and matter was to be remanded for limited purpose of due verification of TDS amounts deducted by deductor and paid to deductee for tax credit claims - Held, yes - Whether due verification of Form 16A, Form 26AS, etc., was to be done and thereafter appropriate relief and benefit be granted to assessee as per law - Held, yes [Para 4.3] [Matter remanded]

FACT: ■

The assessee filed its return for A.Y. 2019-20 declaring income from house property and profits and gains from business or profession and claimed credit of TDS deducted on its receipts.

■

While processing return under section 143(1), CPC Bengaluru computed total income at about Rs. 33.96 lakhs and denied part of TDS credit on ground of mismatch with Form 26AS/AIS. CPC allowed matched TDS credit of about Rs. 6.02 lakhs and disallowed balance TDS of about Rs. 3.64 lakhs, resulting in demand of about Rs. 4.27 lakhs under intimation issued under section 143(1).

■

On first appeal, CIT(A) dismissed appeal holding that TDS credit was governed by section 199 and rule 37BA. CIT(A), after examining Form 26AS, noted that it reflected TDS of about Rs. 6.94 lakhs as against TDS claim of about Rs. 10.58 lakhs in return of income and accordingly upheld CPC’s action in granting credit only to extent reflected in Form 26AS and sustaining disallowance of about Rs. 3.64 lakhs; interest grounds were treated as consequential.

■

On appeal to Tribunal, assessee relied upon Form 16A and Form 26AS placed in paper book to demonstrate that deductor had deducted and deposited TDS, whereas revenue did not object to remand of matter for due verification of TDS records.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal, on the basis of the records of the case and upon examining the rival contentions, is of the considered opinion that the Impugned Order deserves to be set aside as the synopsis and paper book filed demonstrate full payment of TDS by the deductor (supra) in favour of the deductee, the assessee. Under these facts and circumstances, the matter is remanded for the limited purpose of due verification of TDS amounts deducted by the deductor and paid to the deductee for tax credit claims. The due verification of Form 16A, 26AS etc. shall be done and then appropriate relief and benefit shall be granted to the assessee in accordance with law. [Para 4.3]

■

In view of above, the Impugned Order is set aside and the case is remanded back to the file of AO for due verification as directed aforesaid. [Para 4.4]

■

In the result the Impugned Order is set aside as aforesaid with due verification to be done by AO. [Para 5.1]

■

Appeal of the assessee is allowed for statistical purpose. [Para 5.2]

Section 199, read with sections 234B and 234C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Illustrations) - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - During year under consideration, assessee had earned salary income - It had claimed refund of TDS deducted under section 192 - Assessing Officer denied claim of TDS to assessee on ground that same was not reflecting in Form 26AS and consequently, had charged interest under sections 234B and 234C - Whether since assessee himself acting as MD and CEO of its company did not deduct TDS on salary paid/payable to himself for working as MD and CEO of company, he could not be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong and, thus, was not entitled to any claim of set-off of TDS, which was never deposited by company - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 13] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee being managing director and chief executive officer of company himself did not deduct TDS on salary paid/payable to himself for working as MD and CEO of company, he could not be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong and, thus, was not entitled to any claim of set off of TDS which was never deposited by company

Section 205 read with sections 234B and 234C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (General) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee, a salaried employee, filed his income tax return for assessment year 2013-14, reporting a gross salary from its employer-company with TDS deducted - However, a significant discrepancy was found between TDS amount deducted by employer and amount reflected in Form 26AS obtained from Income Tax Department website - Despite tax being deducted, a portion of amount had not been transmitted to Income Tax Department by employer - Consequently, assessee was deprived of receiving credit for full TDS amount, leading to a demand notice issued by income tax department, inclusive of interest under Sections 234B and 234C - Whether in case of an assessee whose tax has been deducted at source but not deposited to Government’s account by deductor, deductee-assessee shall not be called upon to pay demand to extent tax has been deducted from his income - Held, yes - Whether further, section 205 puts a bar on direct demand against assessee in such cases and demand on account of tax credit mismatch in such situations cannot be enforced coercively - Held, yes - Whether therefore, department should not deny benefit of tax deducted at source by employer during relevant financial years to assessee - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 15] [In favour of assessee]

Section 205, read with section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Illustration) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee's employer deducted tax at source while making payment of wages but not deposited to Government Account - Assessing Officer did not grant credit of TDS which had been deducted from wages of assessee - Whether matter was to be restored back to file of Assessing Officer to verify fact and grant set off of tax deducted as well as reflected in salary slip and pass order afresh - Held, yes [Para 4] [Matter remanded]

Section  199  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  390  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Deduction of tax at source – Credit for tax deducted (Short grant of TDS) - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessee claimed that there was a short grant of TDS credit of about Rs. 7.41 lakhs in assessment - Whether assessee was entitled for full credit of TDS and alleged short grant required correction after verification - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, matter was to be restored to file of Assessing Officer to verify facts and pass order in accordance with law - Held, yes [Para 10] [Matter remanded]

Section 205, read with sections 234B and 234BC, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (TDS Credit) - Assessment year 2024-25 - Assessee, an employee, received gross salary from his employer - Employer deducted TDS from his salary but did not issue Form 16 - Assessee filed return declaring salary and claimed said TDS credit - While processing return under section 143(1), CPC denied TDS credit on ground that no corresponding TDS was available in Form 26AS and assessee failed to submit Form 16 and levied interest under sections 234B and 234C - It was noted that employer had not paid any TDS after deducting from employee and after deducting TDS neither remitted amount to Government account nor filed any quarterly returns - Further assessee was an ex-employee and, thus, was not in a position to acquire relevant document from company - Whether since assessee had brought on record relevant salary slips to demonstrate that tax was deducted from salary, revenue could not deny tax credit to assessee - Held, yes - Whether, accordingly, interest levied under sections 234B and 234C was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer had not given any Form 16 to assessee after deducting TDS from salary and assessee had brought on record relevant salary slips to demonstrate that tax was deducted from salary, revenue could not deny tax credit to assessee

Section 220 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection  recovery of tax - When assessee deemed in default - Where Assessing Officer passed order under section 254/143(3) to give effect to order of Tribunal assessing interest income in assessment year 1993-94 but committed a mistake in allowing credit of TDS in assessment year 1992-93 and, therefore, a rectification was made to withdraw credit for TDS for 1992-93 and give credit for such TDS for year 1993-94, interest could not be charged for withdrawal of TDS.

Section 199, read with sections 192 and 205, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - Assessee declared its total income by filing its return of income - Assessee claimed TDS amount deducted by employer from salary - Assessing Officer disallowed claim on ground that employer of assessee had not reflected TDS in Form No. 26AS - Assessee contended that employer had not provided Form No. 16 and he was a regular defaulter - Whether assessee was required to discharge its primary onus by producing relevant documents, then only, it could claim right in its right perspective - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had failed to file any document, wherefrom it could be reflected that assessee had received any particular amount of salary on which TDS had been deducted and therefore, in absence of relevant documents, Commissioner correctly held that Assessing Officer had not made any mistake in non-granting of credit of TDS - Held, yes - Whether however, in absence of relevant documents, issue remained to be adjudicated properly and in its right perspective and therefore, for proper and just decision of case and for end of justice, it was appropriate to remand instant case to file of Commissioner for decision afresh on issue under consideration by giving reasonable opportunity to assessee to produce relevant documents - Held, yes [Paras 6.1 and 6.2] [Matter remanded]

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with rule 37BA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Bank confirmation letter) - Assessment year 2022-23 - Assessee, a foreign company, was engaged in investment activities managed from out of India - Assessee was a beneficial owner of American Depository Receipts (ADRs) of V Ltd., which were held through a broker - Thereafter, ADRs were compulsorily redeemed by Citibank, acting as depository participant for V ltd. - Upon redemption, Citibank NA withheld tax at 43.68 per cent on gross proceeds as assessee did not have PAN - Later, assessee after obtaining PAN filed revised return and claimed TDS credit - Assessing Officer denied said claim of assessee on ground that TDS was not reflected in Form 26AS - Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld same on ground that assessee's non-compliance with rule 37BA was a sufficient basis for denial of TDS credit and dismissed appeal - It was noted that due to absence of assessee's PAN at time of deduction, TDS credit was incorrectly attributed under category 'without PAN' or in name of broker, CS , rather than assessee and this misattribution led to TDS credit not reflecting in assessee's Form 26AS - It was also noted that upon obtaining a PAN, assessee actively engaged with Citibank NA and CS AG to correct TDS attribution -However, despite continuous communication and submission of necessary documents, including confirmations, these procedural corrections were not completed in time to reflect in assessee's Form 26AS at stage of assessment - Whether a taxpayer should not suffer due to procedural lapses caused by third parties, especially when taxpayer had acted in good faith and made all reasonable efforts to rectify situation - Held, yes - Whether substance of compliance, namely offering income to tax, should take precedence over procedural errors when assessing a taxpayer's entitlement to TDS credit - Held, yes - Whether TDS credit, once deducted, should not be denied based on procedural failures, particularly those not attributable to taxpayer - Held, yes - Whether thus, assessee was entitled to TDS credit as claimed - Held, yes [Paras 6.6 and 6.7] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where due to absence of assessee’s PAN at time of redemption of ADRs, tax was withheld on income earned by assessee, and was incorrectly attributed under category without PAN or in name of broker, since assessee obtained PAN and claimed TDS credit in revised return, TDS credit could not be denied on procedural ground that TDS was not reflected in Form 26AS due to non-compliance with rule 37BA by third parties

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with rule 37BA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Bank confirmation letter) - Assessment year 2022-23 - Assessee, a foreign company, was engaged in investment activities managed from out of India - Assessee was a beneficial owner of American Depository Receipts (ADRs) of V Ltd., which were held through a broker - Thereafter, ADRs were compulsorily redeemed by Citibank, acting as depository participant for V ltd. - Upon redemption, Citibank NA withheld tax at 43.68 per cent on gross proceeds as assessee did not have PAN - Later, assessee after obtaining PAN filed revised return and claimed TDS credit - Assessing Officer denied said claim of assessee on ground that TDS was not reflected in Form 26AS - Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld same on ground that assessee's non-compliance with rule 37BA was a sufficient basis for denial of TDS credit and dismissed appeal - It was noted that due to absence of assessee's PAN at time of deduction, TDS credit was incorrectly attributed under category 'without PAN' or in name of broker, CS , rather than assessee and this misattribution led to TDS credit not reflecting in assessee's Form 26AS - It was also noted that upon obtaining a PAN, assessee actively engaged with Citibank NA and CS AG to correct TDS attribution -However, despite continuous communication and submission of necessary documents, including confirmations, these procedural corrections were not completed in time to reflect in assessee's Form 26AS at stage of assessment - Whether a taxpayer should not suffer due to procedural lapses caused by third parties, especially when taxpayer had acted in good faith and made all reasonable efforts to rectify situation - Held, yes - Whether substance of compliance, namely offering income to tax, should take precedence over procedural errors when assessing a taxpayer's entitlement to TDS credit - Held, yes - Whether TDS credit, once deducted, should not be denied based on procedural failures, particularly those not attributable to taxpayer - Held, yes - Whether thus, assessee was entitled to TDS credit as claimed - Held, yes [Paras 6.6 and 6.7] [In favour of assessee]

III. Section  199  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  390  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Deduction of tax at source – Credit for tax deducted (General) - Assessment year  2011-12  - Whether credit for TDS cannot be denied where corresponding income has been duly offered to tax by assessee and tax deducted at source is duly reflected in relevant records - Held, yes - Whether where assessee had placed reliance on updated Form 26AS and had also sought verification of corresponding income offered to tax, matter was to be restored to file of Assessing Officer for verification and grant of appropriate TDS credit in accordance with law – Held, yes [Paras 9.1 and 9.2] [Matter remanded]

Section 199, read with section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Credit of TDS) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was an employee of Indian Railways - He had received salary income but had not filed his return of income - Accordingly, Assessing Officer passed an assessment order under section 144 and made addition to assessee's income based on salary received by assessee as reflected in Form 26AS - Assessee contended that TDS was deducted from his salary which was duly reflected in Form 26AS, therefore, matter should be remanded back to Assessing Officer for verification of facts and to allow credit of TDS - It was noted that addition in case of assessee was made by Assessing Officer based on income of assessee reflected in Form 26AS, but TDS credit available in Form 26AS was not allowed to assessee - Whether since legitimate credit of TDS was not allowed by Assessing Officer, in spite of having such facts on records, there was perversity in order of Assessing Officer and therefore, matter was to be remanded back to Assessing Officer for fresh adjudication - Held, yes [Para 8] [Matter remanded]

Section 199, read with section 205, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit of tax deducted (Burden of proof) - Assessment years 2008-11 and 2014-15 - Whether for availing credit of TDS, assessee-payee has to discharge its responsibility of substantiating whether tax was deducted by payer of income - Held, yes - Whether where assessee-payee had neither furnished any details of amount of TDS in respect of interest income, which it had shown if any in its profit and loss account, nor furnished any evidence to support deduction of tax at source by payer of income, issue of granting credit of tax deducted at source was to be restored to file of Assessing Officer for verification as to whether assessee had shown interest income corresponding to TDS in profit and loss account for year under consideration and whether tax had been deducted at source by payer of income - Held, yes - Whether Assessing Officer need not insist on demand in respect of said TDS payment to Government account - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [Matter remanded]INCOME TAX : For availing credit of TDS, assessee-payee has to discharge its responsibility of substantiating whether tax was deducted by payer of income

Section  199,  read with section  205,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Credit for tax deducted  (Scope of provision) - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessee let out his flat to a company under a leave and license agreement - Licensee deducted TDS from rent receipts but did not deposit part of it - Assessing Officer declined TDS credit to assessee to extent of shortfall on ground that same was not reflected in Form 26AS - It was noted that assessee had submitted necessary evidence like copies of ITR, computation, statement in Form 26AS, leave and license agreement, bank statement to support facts of case - Furthermore, revenue had not doubted fact that tax was deducted at source but was not deposited by deductor - Whether thus, Assessing Officer was directed to allow credit of TDS after due verification of facts on record - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]

Section 199, read with section 205, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit of tax deducted (Burden of proof) - Assessment years 2008-11 and 2014-15 - Whether for availing credit of TDS, assessee-payee has to discharge its responsibility of substantiating whether tax was deducted by payer of income - Held, yes - Whether where assessee-payee had neither furnished any details of amount of TDS in respect of interest income, which it had shown if any in its profit and loss account, nor furnished any evidence to support deduction of tax at source by payer of income, issue of granting credit of tax deducted at source was to be restored to file of Assessing Officer for verification as to whether assessee had shown interest income corresponding to TDS in profit and loss account for year under consideration and whether tax had been deducted at source by payer of income - Held, yes - Whether Assessing Officer need not insist on demand in respect of said TDS payment to Government account - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [Matter remanded]   Circulars and Notifications: CBDT's OM F/No. 275/29/2014-IT(B), dated 11-3-2016

III. Section  199  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  390  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Deduction of tax at source – Credit for tax deducted (TDS/TCS credit) - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessee claimed TDS credit of about Rs. 71.86 lakhs and TCS credit of about Rs. 0.91 lakhs in its return - Assessment order did not grant full credit as claimed - Whether since grant of TDS/TCS credit is consequential and verification based, issue was to be restored to file of Assessing Officer with a direction to verify assessee's claim from Form 26AS/AIS and other supporting evidences and grant due credit in accordance with law - Held, yes [Para 13] [Matter remanded]

Section 205, read with  section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Scope of provision) - Assessment years 2009-10, 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Employer paid salary to assessee after deduction of tax at source but did not deposit same with department - Assessing Officer did not allow credit of tax deducted at source and raised demand against assessee towards tax and interest - Whether assessee having accepted salary after deduction of tax at source had no further control over it and it was duty of employer to pay deducted tax to department and employer having failed to perform his duty to deposit deducted tax, assessee could not be penalized - Held, yes - Whether section 199 could not operate as impediment to grant relief to assessee and, thus, impugned demand deserved to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Instruction No. 275, dated 1-6-2015; Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016 and Press Release, dated 11-3-2016

II. Section 201 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  398  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -Deduction of tax at source - Consequence of failure to deduct or pay (Illustrations) - Assessment year 2018-19 - Assessee, a real estate concern, filed tax audit report in Form 3CA/Form 3CD - Relying on audit report, Assessing Officer noted that assessee had not deducted tax on certain expenses which were eligible for TDS - Accordingly, Assessing Officer treated assessee as an assessee in default under section 201 - Assessee contended that in respect of other expenses on which TDS was not deducted, occasion had not arisen as provisions had not been crystallized and, therefore, responsibility to deduct tax would arise only when assessee was required to pay income and not on provisions - Assessee submitted that provisions reported in Form 3CD had been crystallized in subsequent years and necessary TDS had also been deducted at source - Further, assessee also submitted that in some cases, TDS was also deducted and remitted to department - Whether it would be open to assessee to adduce further evidences to show that deduction of TDS was not required or deduction was made and tax was remitted to department and, thus, Assessing Officer was to be directed to consider documents and arrive a conclusion that whether assessee was to be treated as assessee-in-default or not - Held, yes [Para 9] [Matter remanded]

Section 199, read with sections 192 and 205, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - Assessee declared its total income by filing its return of income - Assessee claimed TDS amount deducted by employer from salary - Assessing Officer disallowed claim on ground that employer of assessee had not reflected TDS in Form No. 26AS - Assessee contended that employer had not provided Form No. 16 and he was a regular defaulter - Whether assessee was required to discharge its primary onus by producing relevant documents, then only, it could claim right in its right perspective - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had failed to file any document, wherefrom it could be reflected that assessee had received any particular amount of salary on which TDS had been deducted and therefore, in absence of relevant documents, Commissioner correctly held that Assessing Officer had not made any mistake in non-granting of credit of TDS - Held, yes - Whether however, in absence of relevant documents, issue remained to be adjudicated properly and in its right perspective and therefore, for proper and just decision of case and for end of justice, it was appropriate to remand instant case to file of Commissioner for decision afresh on issue under consideration by giving reasonable opportunity to assessee to produce relevant documents - Held, yes [Paras 6.1 and 6.2] [Matter remanded]INCOME TAX : Where assessee claimed TDS amount deducted by employer from salary and Assessing Officer denied claim on ground that employer of assessee had not reflected TDS in Form 26AS, however assessee alleged that his employer had not provided him Form No. 16 and was a regular defaulter, in view of fact that assessee failed to file any document to substantiate his claim, matter was to be remanded to Commissioner for decision afresh

I. Section 201, read with sections 194A and 201(1A), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Consequences of failure to deduct or pay (Illustrations) - Assessment year 2019-20 - Assessee-company was engaged in development of residential apartments, hotels and educational institutions - During year, assessee made several payments but there was no remitance of TDS deducted - Assessing Officer was of view that assessee had not deducted TDS on these payments thus, he treated assessee as assessee-in-default - Assessee contended that it was in serious financial crisis due to which TDS deducted on payments could not be remitted into Government account and an opportunity should be given to produce Form 26A to evidence that payee to whom amounts were credited had included same in their return of income and duly paid tax thereon - Whether, on facts, assessee should be given an opportunity to prove whether payees had paid taxes due and, accordingly, matter was to be remanded to Assessing Officer to consider evidences that assessee would produce in support of its abovesaid contention that payees had paid taxes due with respect to amount credited by assessee and decide case on merits in accordance with law - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee-company contended that it was in serious financial crisis due to which TDS deducted could not be remitted into Government account and an opportunity should be given to produce Form 26A to show that payees to whom amounts were credited had included same in their return of income and duly paid tax thereon, assessee should be given an opportunity to prove whether payees had paid taxes due, and, accordingly, matter was to be remanded to AO to consider evidences that assessee would produce in support of its abovesaid contention   INCOME TAX : When buyer/borrower being person responsible to making interest payment was not liable to deduct tax at source under section 194A assessee-real estate developer, who was making pre-EMI interest on behalf of buyer/borrower could not be held to be liable to deduct tax at source

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Scope of provision) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee had provided services to an entity - Said entity had deducted tax at source on amount paid to assessee - However tax at source deducted by said entity was not completely deposited with revenue and therefore, assessee was not given credit for tax deducted at source by said entity - Assessee averred that instead of being granted credit for tax deducted at source by said entity, revenue raised a demand against it - Whether revenue could not recover deficit tax at source from assessee, which was deducted and pocketed by entity in question, and they could not also refuse to grant credit for same - Held, yes - Whether therefore, revenue would refund to assessee as prayed - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 15] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee had provided services to an entity and said entity had deducted tax at source on amount paid to assessee but had not completely deposited said tax, in said circumstances, revenue could not recover deficit tax at source from assessee, which was deducted and pocketed by entity in question, and thus revenue could not also refuse to grant credit for same

Section  199,  read with section  143,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  390,  read with section  270  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Deduction of tax at source – Credit for tax deducted (Illustrations) - Assessment year  2019-20  - Assessee filed return declaring total income of about Rs. 33.96 lakhs - On processing return under section 143(1), CPC raised demand of about Rs. 4.27 lakhs after allowing matched TDS credit of about Rs. 6.02 lakhs and treating balance TDS claim of about Rs. 3.65 lakhs as mismatched - CIT(A) upheld denial of TDS credit holding that credit under section 199 read with Rule 37BA is allowable on basis of Form 26AS/TDS certificates - Whether since assessee, on basis of synopsis and paper book, demonstrated full payment of TDS by deductor in favour of deductee assessee, impugned order deserved to be set aside and matter was to be remanded for limited purpose of due verification of TDS amounts deducted by deductor and paid to deductee for tax credit claims - Held, yes - Whether due verification of Form 16A, Form 26AS, etc., was to be done and thereafter appropriate relief and benefit be granted to assessee as per law - Held, yes [Para 4.3] [Matter remanded]

Section 205, read with  section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Scope of provision) - Assessment years 2009-10, 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Employer paid salary to assessee after deduction of tax at source but did not deposit same with department - Assessing Officer did not allow credit of tax deducted at source and raised demand against assessee towards tax and interest - Whether assessee having accepted salary after deduction of tax at source had no further control over it and it was duty of employer to pay deducted tax to department and employer having failed to perform his duty to deposit deducted tax, assessee could not be penalized - Held, yes - Whether section 199 could not operate as impediment to grant relief to assessee and, thus, impugned demand deserved to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer paid salary to assessee after deduction of tax at source but employer did not deposit same with department, assessee could not be penalized for failure of employer to perform his duty to deposit deducted tax

Section  205  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee  (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year  2020-21 and 2021-22  - Employer of assessee deducted tax at source from salary income of assessee for two years but did not deposit same with Government - When assessee filed return of income disclosing tax deducted at source, there was a mismatch in system and accordingly, demand was raised upon assessee by an intimation issued under section 143(1) - High Court held that since there was failure on part of employer to deposit tax deducted at source from salary income of assessee, revenue could not have raised any demand against assessee in view of provisions of section 205 read with  Instruction No. 275 dated 01.06.2015  and Office Memorandum dated 11.03.2016 - It was noted that common order passed by High Court had already been considered in a connected matter in Income-tax Assessing Officer, Baroda v. Shobhan Shantilal Doshi [2026] 182 taxmann.com 555 (SC), and same was disposed of by clarifying directions given with reference to changes to be made in software - Whether in view of directions already issued, no further order was required to be passed in impugned petition and, thus, SLP was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 3 and 4] [In favour of assessee]

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year 2020-21 and 2021-22 - Employer of assessee deducted tax at source from salary income of assessee for two years but did not deposit same with Government - When assessee filed return of income disclosing tax deducted at source, there was a mismatch in system and accordingly, demand was raised upon assessee by an intimation issued under section 143(1) - Whether since there was failure on part of employer to deposit tax deducted at source from salary income of assessee, revenue could not have raised any demand against assessee in view of provisions of section 205 read with Instruction No. 275 dated 01.06.2015 and Office Memorandum dated 11.03.2016 - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 10] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Instruction No. 275, dated 1-6-2015 and Office Memorandum F. No. 275/29/2014-IT(B), dated 11-3-2016.

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Tax deducted at source) - Assessment years  2009-10  and 2011-12 - Assessee was employed with company KIL - During course of employment, KIL deducted TDS from assessee's salary but, KIL did not deposit same with Income-tax authorities - Accordingly, revenue raised demand against assessee - Assessee claimed that TDS was duly reflected in Form 16A issued by KIL and, thus, he was not liable to pay tax - Whether in view of decision in case of Sanjay Sudan v. Asstt. CIT [2023] 148 taxmann.com 329/292 Taxman 138/452 ITR 107 (Delhi), revenue could not recover TDS from assessee - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]

VIII. Section  199  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 /  Section  390   of the Income-tax Act, 2025 - Deduction of tax at source – Credit for tax deducted (Short grant of credit) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee claimed TDS credit of Rs. 52.23 crores in return, matching Form 26AS, but AO allowed Rs. 52.21 crores, resulting in a short grant of Rs. 1.81 lakhs - Assessee sought verification and grant of balance TDS credit before Tribunal - Whether AO was to be directed to look into issue and grant appropriate relief to assessee - Held, yes [Para 37] [Matter remanded]

Section  205,  read with section  199,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee  (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year  2020-21 and 2021-22  - Assessee’s employer deducted tax at source from salary but failed to deposit same with Government - While processing return, Assessing Officer denied credit of such TDS to assessee due to system mismatch and raised demand - High Court held that in view of section 205 read with CBDT  Instruction No. 275 dated 1-6-2015  and Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016, no demand could be raised against assessee where tax had been deducted but not deposited by the deductor - High Court further directed CBDT to modify software so that no demand could be raised in future in cases where there would be mismatch between TDS and tax not deposited by deductor in case of deductee - Whether since aforesaid directions had nothing to do with case on merits and would not affect assessee, direction issued for changes to be made in software were to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 5] [Partly in favour of revenue]

Section 205, read with sections 192, 199 and 203, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection and recovery of tax - Bar against direct demand on assessee - Assessment year 1996-97 - Whether in view of section 205, income-tax authorities, under no circumstances, can make assessee liable to make payment of any tax to extent to which tax has been deducted at source by person paying salary to assessee under section 192 - Held, yes - Whether, however, at same time, credit for tax deducted at source cannot be given to assessee unless he submits certificate as prescribed under section 203 in 
 respect of TDS as per provisions of section 199 - Held, yes - Whether till powers available to income-tax authorities to enforce payment of tax by deductor and also enforce issue of certificate in respect thereof to payee were not exercised by revenue authorities to corner deductor of tax, no tax as well as interest pertaining thereto could be recovered from assessee - Held, yes.

facts.text:
■

The assessee was an employee of company, D. The employer had deducted TDS from monthly salary of the assessee, however, same was not deposited to the Government. The assessee filed return and claimed TDS as pre-paid taxes.

■

The Assessing Officer denied assessee's claim.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) restored the matter back to the file of the Assessing Officer directing him to verify the claim of the assessee from Form 26AS and ITR and if the claim was found to be correct, an appropriate amount of TDS credit be allowed to the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee, an employee, received salary on which TDS was deducted. However, the employer had not deposited the TDS to the account of the Central Government.

■

The assessee had filed his return of income and claimed credit of the TDS that was deducted in the salary.

■

In the intimation issued, the credit of the TDS had not been granted and a demand was raised against the assessee in lieu of the credit of the TDS not granted.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee–employee filed a return declaring total income of about Rs. 70.37 lakhs for the year under consideration and claimed TDS credit of about Rs. 18.10 lakhs.

■

The return was processed under section 143(1) by CPC, which allowed TDS credit of about Rs. 0.60 lakhs only, restricting the balance claim.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the AO to grant an opportunity of being heard, verify the TDS with Form 26AS and other relevant material to ascertain whether it related to the income offered in the year, and thereafter grant credit if the claim was found correct.

■
