65. Yearly comparision to be made of credit shown in Form GSTR-2B with credit in Form GSTR-3B.

The current manner of availing the credit and verification is as follows:

Section 16(2) of the CGST Act prescribes the condition for availment of credit. The major conditions are that the recipient should have received the goods or services and that copies of invoices or other documents evidencing payment of tax are available with the recipient.

The supplier of goods or services is required to declare the supply in GSTR-1 every month or Form GSTR-1 through IFF quarterly. The information stated in this form, inter-alia, includes the registration number of the recipient.

The portal prepares a statement of input tax credit for each registered person (recipient) in Form GSTR-2B, which should be availed as credit for that month as per the circular issued by the department.

In case of a difference in the amount of credit for any month shown in Form GSTR-3B with the amount in Form GSTR-2B, notice is issued to the recipient.

The recipient does not avail of the credit unless the invoice is accounted for in the books of accounts. This section presumes that the invoice of the supplier is accounted for in the books of account in the same month in which the supplier raises the invoice. Say the supplier has raised the invoice in the month of Nov-2024 for supplies made in Nov-2024. It is presumed by the above method that the invoice will be accounted for by the recipient in Nov-2024, and he will avail the credit in the same month.

As per Section 16(4) of the CGST Act, the recipient can avail of the credit of GST by November following the end of the financial year. Thus, credit for the supply of Nov-2024 can be availed latest by 30th November 2025. Further, the annual return in Form GSTR-9 and Form GSTR-9C is required to be filed by December following the end of the financial year. Therefore, monitoring the availment of credit on a monthly basis when the law permits availment in subsequent months is leading to substantial problems and unnecessary issues of letters.

The department should compare the availment of credit on a yearly basis as against a monthly basis. The format of Form GSTR-9 and Form GSTR-9C shall be suitably amended to provide all the information desired by the department so that the verification in the audit is minimal.

Doctrine of Unjust Enrichment

8. The resolution plan cannot provide for extinguishment of the liability of the corporate debtor in respect of amounts deducted or collected as fiduciary of the statutory authorities. One example is tax deducted at source; other common example is indirect tax.

Such an amount cannot be said to be forming a part of the estate of the corporate debtor. The resolution applicant who submits resolution plan intends to acquire the corporate debtor at the best (read, lowest) possible price. However, extinguishment of amounts as aforesaid will lead to what is commonly referred to as "unjust enrichment" of the shareholders of the acquirer, that too at the cost of the persons who suffered taxes.

In K. Logachandran v. District Collector [2010] 157 Comp Cases 686, it was held by the Hon'ble Madras High Court-

As is evident from the discussion so far, plans or schemes approved under statutes have been given overriding effect, so as to be called "a statutory magic"; however, a pre-condition is that the same shall "legitimately" bind those who dissented to the scheme/plan. (i)

Statutory dues cannot be reduced or extinguished without seeking consent of the concerned authority. (ii)

The above holds true even if statutory dues are deferred or scheduled to paid in tranches.

(iii)

The resolution plan shall, at bare minimum, provide for payment of liquidation value due towards statutory dues. The plan cannot go beyond such minimum level. See "Guide to Liquidation Value under the Insolvency Code"7, by Sikha Bansal.

(iv)

In case of statutory arrears, the retention of which leads to unjust enrichment of the corporate debtor, waiver/extinguishment is not possible.

9. Time-limit may be specified for passing an order in case of TDS default from the payment made to non-resident

As per section 201 of the Income-tax Act, if a person responsible for deduction of tax at source, fails to deduct the whole or any part of the tax or after deduction fails to deposit the same to the credit of the Central Government, then he shall be deemed to be an assessee-in-default. Sub-section (3) of said section provides that no order deeming a deductor to be an assessee-in-default shall be passed after expiry of 7 years from the end of the financial year in which payment is made, or credit is given or after expiry of 2 years from the end of the financial year in which correction statement is furnished, whichever is later. However, these time limits are applicable only when TDS defaults are related to payments made to a person resident in India. In other words, sub-section (3) does not apply if there is a TDS default with respect to payments made to a non-resident.

As no time-limit has been prescribed under the Act for passing an order against a person who defaults in deducting or depositing tax with respect to payments made to a non-resident, various Courts have held that the action can be taken by the department in a reasonable time but what should be the reasonable time, is quite controversial.

Hence, the Government may make a necessary amendment under sub-section (3) of section 201 to specify the time-limit for passing an order of assessee-in-default where a person makes default in deducting or depositing tax in respect of payments made to a non-resident. It is expected that the Govt. may bring both the provisions in parity.

10. Long-term capital gains taxable under Sec. 112A should be excluded from the charging provisions of section 115UA

Section 115UA provides how the income of a Business trust and its unitholders shall be charged to tax. It provides that total income of a business trust shall be taxable at the maximum marginal rate. However, total income excludes income which is taxable as per the provisions of section 111A and Section 112.

The Finance Act, 2018, inserted a new Section 112A in the Income-tax Act which provides for the taxability of income arising from the transfer of a long term capital asset, being a listed equity share or a unit of an equity oriented fund or a unit of a business trust.

Section 112A provides a special rate of 10% at which the long term capital gains arising from the transfer of above capital assets shall be charged to tax. However, section 115UA does not contain any exception in respect of section 112A.

Thus, it is recommended that an amendment should be made to Section 115UA to exclude the long-term capital gains as referred to in section 112A from the charging provisions of section 115UA. This amendment is necessary to give the same treatment to Section 112A capital gains as given to capital gains referred to in Section 111A and Section 112.

11. Rules for expeditious hearing of Special bench cases

The Income-tax Tribunal is the last fact-finding appellate authority under the Income-tax Act. The appeals filed before the Tribunals are heard by the division bench- consisting of one judicial member and one accountant member.

In case of conflict of opinions by the division benches on the issues involved in an appeal, the appeals are sometimes heard by the special benches consisting of three or more members and at least one of them must be a judicial member and at least one of them must be an accountant member.

Recently, we have witnessed a ruling wherein the Tribunal was unhappy with the approach followed by the members of a special bench to dispose of an appeal. The Ahmedabad Tribunal in the case of Doshi Accounting Services (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2019] 101 taxmann.com 62 (Ahmedabad - Trib.) (SB)had formulated the following guidelines to ensure the expeditious hearing of cases referred to Special Benches and Third Members:

(a)

The special benches shall commence hearing within 120 days of its constitution. In case of any delay, it shall record the reasons in brief;

(b)

The adjournment may be granted only in exceptional circumstances which shall not be of more than 30 days at the instance of either party; and

(c)

The above guidelines shall also be followed with respect to Third Member cases, and the Registry will take up the matter with the respective benches for scheduling the hearing.

It is expected that the Govt. could make necessary amendments to Section 255 for expediting the hearing in Special Benches.

Section 254(2A) of the Act contains provisions for the disposal of appeals by the Tribunal. The first proviso to Section 254(2A) provides that if an assessee makes an application for the stay of proceedings, the Tribunal may, after considering the merits of the application, pass an order of stay for a period not exceeding 180 days from the date of the order. The Tribunal shall dispose of the proceedings within that period of stay. Where the Tribunal does not dispose of the appeal within the original period of stay, and the delay is not attributable to the assessee, the Tribunal may extend the period of stay for a total period of 365 days (365 days including 180 days granted previously).

Further, the third proviso to Section 254(2A) provides that if the Tribunal does not dispose of the appeal within the period allowed (original plus extended), the order of stay shall stand vacated after the expiry of 365 days even if the delay in disposing of the appeal is not attributable to the assessee.

In Dy. CIT v. Pepsi Foods Ltd. [2021] 126 taxmann.com 69 (SC), the Supreme Courthas held that the object of the third proviso to Section 254(2A) (i.e., automatic vacation of stay on completion of 365 days even if the assessee is not responsible for the delay) is discriminatory and is liable to be struck down as it violates Article 14 of the Constitution of India. The Apex Court further held that the third proviso should be read without the word "even" and "is not". Thus, any order of stay shall stand vacated after the expiry of the mentioned period only if the delay in disposing of the appeal is attributable to the assessee. After these words are struck down, the third proviso shall be read as under:

Provided also that if such appeal is not so disposed of within the period allowed under the first proviso or the period or periods extended or allowed under the second proviso, which shall not, in any case, exceed three hundred and sixty-five days, the order of stay shall stand vacated after the expiry of such period or periods, even if the delay in disposing of the appeal is not attributable to the assessee.

Thus, it is expected that the Govt. may bring an amendment in the third proviso to Section 254(2A) as held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the above case.

49. Tax recovery mechanism on sale of securitised assets

Securitisation is a process that allows banks and other financial institutions to auction properties to recover the loan amount on the borrower's failure to repay.

In most cases where the assets are taken over as part of the recovery of borrowing, there is no mechanism to ensure that the tax dues are secured in the process of the sale of properties.

The borrower has no money to pay the tax as he is already bankrupt or faces financial difficulties. Further, no part of the sale consideration reaches him as sale proceeds are collected directly by the bank or Asset Reconstruction Company (ARC). The banks or ARCs have no statutory obligations to make payments of taxes levied on the borrower.

The Mumbai Tribunal7 has also highlighted this legal lacuna in tax recovery on the sale of securitised assets. Thus, it is recommended that the Government brings a suitable amendment to ensure that the tax liability is duly recovered from the borrower whose property is sold. Alternatively, it may be provided that if it is not possible to recover tax from the borrower due to financial difficulties, the tax dues may be recovered from the bank/ARC.

The Finance Act, 2018 has provided that trusts or institutions will also be required to follow the provisions of TDS and will make all expenses in excess of Rs. 10,000 through banking channels. 24. Notional interest on security deposit received by landlord for letting out the property

Deposit of security amount is a usual practice at the time of letting out a property. There is no provision in the Income-tax Act to calculate and include the notional interest on such security amount while calculating the income from house property.

The Courts have consistently held that notional interest on interest free security deposit shall not be taken into consideration while computing ALV of house property let out by the taxpayers.

It is suggested that the upcoming Budget should bring suitable amendments to end the litigations on this count. If the security deposit is reasonable (equivalent to average rent for 3 months) no notional interest should be added to the income from house property.

25. Meaning of the term 'Month' and computation thereof

As per the provisions of section 201(1A), in case of failure to deduct TDS, interest is to be paid at the rate of 1.5% from the date of deduction to the date of payment. Any part of the month shall be considered as one full month. So, the understanding should be that if TDS is deducted on April 23, 2019 and payment is made on 8th May, 2019, interest should be paid for one month.

However, Income-tax Dept. calculates interest for 2 months because it considers April and May as two separate calendar months. So, the scenario is that even if the TDS is late by 1 day, interest is calculated for 2 months which seems to be an absurd situation.

The ITAT in the case of Bank of Baroda v. DCIT [2017] 88 taxmann.com 103 (Ahmedabad - Trib.) also held that interest was to be levied only for actual period of delay, i.e., from date on which tax was deducted and till date on which tax was deposited. If such a period exceeded one month then full month's interest was leviable. It is very common problem that every deductor faces in all those provisions where interest or fees is calculated in reference to 'month' of default. Thus, it would be advisable that Income-tax Act should explicitly define the meaning of the expression 'month'.

26. Deductibility of discount given on ESOPs

Some of recent judicial pronouncements suggest that the tax fraternity is grappling with the controversy on the tax treatment of the discounts on the shares issued to the employees under ESOPs.

The revenue has been contending that the said discounts can never be allowed as deductions on the following grounds:

At the most, such discount could be considered as a short capital receipt or a sort of capital expenditure.

Conversely, the Companies issuing ESOP's argue that the primary object of an ESOP is not to raise share capital but to earn profit by securing the consistent and concentrated efforts of its dedicated employees during the vesting period. Such discounted premium on shares is a substitute for giving direct incentive in cash for availing of the services of the employees.

In order to avoid unnecessary litigations, it would be prudent for the Finance Minister to clarify this stand on the tax treatment of discounts on issue of shares under ESOP. The industry expects a clarification stating that the discounts on ESOP scheme should be amortized over the vesting period.

25. TDS on Salary and Provident Fund

As per ITA 1961

Section 192 governs TDS on salary. It mandates tax deduction at the average rate on the estimated income under the head "Salaries" at the time of payment.

Sub-section (6) of Section 192 specifically deals with the valuation of salary paid in foreign currency, stating that such salary must be converted into Indian Rupees at the prescribed exchange rates for the purpose of TDS.

Further, Section 192A mandates 10% TDS on taxable payments from recognised provident funds, where the accumulated balance is included in total income and is Rs. 50,000 or more. This section contains a non-obstante clause, meaning it overrides other provisions of the Act.

As per ITB 2025

Clause 392 of the Bill consolidates the provisions of Sections 192 and 192A.

(a)

Sub-clauses (1) to (6) of Clause 392 provide for TDS on salary at the average rate, based on estimated income for the tax year. However, there is no provision corresponding to the current Section 192(6) regarding salary paid in foreign currency.

(b)

Clause 392(7) provides for 10% TDS on the accumulated balance withdrawn from a recognised provident fund, where such amount is taxable and is Rs. 50,000 or more. Unlike Section 192A, this clause does not contain a non-obstante clause.

Select Committee Recommendation

(a)

Clarity on TDS rate for recognised provident fund

The Committee observed that Clause 392(7)(a) lacked clarity on whether TDS should apply at the average rate (as used for salary under Clause 392(1)) or at the flat rate of 10% (as stated in Clause 392(7)).To avoid misinterpretation and ensure consistency with current law, the Committee recommended inserting a non-obstante clause to clarify that 10% TDS shall apply in such cases. The Ministry accepted this recommendation.

(b)

Inclusion of a provision for salary paid in foreign currency

The Committee noted that the Bill inadvertently omitted provisions corresponding to Section 192(6), which governs the conversion of foreign currency salary into INR at prescribed rates for TDS purposes.

The absence of such a provision could lead to inconsistent valuation, confusion, and potential litigation. The Committee recommended that a suitable provision be inserted in Clause 392 to prescribe conversion at the notified forex rates. The Ministry also accepted this recommendation.

26. Certificate for lower or nil deduction /collection of tax

Clause 395 of the ITB consolidates and simplifies several provisions of the ITA, such as Sections 195(2), 197, 197A, 203, 206C(9), and 206C(10), which relate to certificates for lower or nil deduction/collection of tax.

The Committee noted that Clause 395(1) removes the term "Nil deduction" which is explicitly present in Section 197 of the existing Act. The Department stated that "lower deduction" is meant to include "nil deduction" as well, and that clarification will be issued via administrative instructions. However, the Committee felt that replacing "nil" with "lower" may lead to ambiguity, especially in practical cases such as foreign banks seeking exemption from TDS on customer payments or loss-making entities or non-residents availing of treaty benefits.

To avoid confusion and ensure clarity in law, the Committee recommended that the word "nil" be reinstated in Clause 395(1), rather than relying on future administrative guidance.

This ensures that powers are territorially restricted to prevent overreach.

Time-limit may be specified for passing an order in case of default in deduction of tax from the payment made to non-resident As per Section 201 of the Income-tax Act, if a person responsible for deduction of tax at source, fails to deduct the whole or any part of the tax or after deduction fails to deposit the same to the credit of the Central Government, then he shall be deemed to be an assessee-in-default.

Sub-section (3) of Section 201 provides that no order deeming a deductor to be an assessee-in-default, on failure to deduct the tax from a person resident in India, shall be passed after expiry of 7 years from the end of the financial year in which payment is made, or credit is given or after the expiry of 2 years from the end of the financial year in which correction statement is furnished, whichever is later. However, these time limits are applicable only when TDS defaults are related to payments made to a person resident in India. In other words, sub-section (3) does not apply if there is a default in deduction of tax with respect to payments made to a non-resident.

As no time-limit has been prescribed under the Act for passing an order against a person who defaults in deducting or depositing tax with respect to payments made to a non-resident, various courts have held that the action can be taken by the department in a reasonable time but what should be a reasonable time, is quite controversial.

Hence, the Government may make a necessary amendment under sub-section (3) of section 201 to specify the time-limit for passing an order of assessee-in-default where a person makes default in deducting or depositing tax in respect of payments made to a non-resident. deduction of tax at source. We want to know whether education cess is payable on such TDS?

The issue is quite complicated, since it involves various aspects. Before I attempt to answer the question, some points must be noted, to make our thinking clear :

lIn some cases, service tax is payable under reverse charge method under section 68(2) of the Finance Act, 1994, i.e., though tax liability is of service provider, the payment liability is of service receiver. lHowever, in case of non-resident service provider, the tax liability is on service receiver under section 66A(1) of the Finance Act, 1994 with effect from 1-5-2006 [earlier Explanation to section 65(105) during the period 16-6-2005 to 30-4-2006].

lThis section states that service receiver shall be treated as service provider and directly casts responsibility for payment of service tax on him. Thus, it is not that initially the liability is on service provider which is then shifted to service receiver under section 68(2) of the Finance Act, 1994.

lThus, a foreign person is never liable to make any payment towards service tax. It is not that the amount is payable to the non-resident and instead of paying it to him or by deducting from amount payable to him, the Indian resident is liable to make payment to Government.

lSection 195 of the Income-tax Act requires that TDS should be on interest or any other sum chargeable under provisions of the Income-tax Act. Tax is to be deducted at the time of credit of such income to the account of the payee.

lAs explained above, the amount of service tax is never credited to the account of payee.

lIn case of Double Tax Avoidance Agreement (DTAA), provisions of DTAA prevail over provisions of Income-tax Act - CBDT Circular No. 333, dated 2-4-1982 - view confirmed in Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan [2003] = 132 Taxman 373 = 263 ITR 706 (SC).

lDTAA applies to all taxes on income by whatever name called. All DTA agreements provide that it shall apply to any identical or substantially similar taxes which are imposed after the date of signature of the DTA in addition to, or in place of, the existing taxes.

lEducation cess on Income-tax is also Income-tax.

lThe DTAA prescribes overall limit for deducting tax at source.

In view of above, my answers would be as follows -

(a)TDS is not required to be deducted on service tax which is paid directly to Government.

(b)In case of DTAA, the percentage for TDS is total. Hence, education cess is not required to be paid. However, in case of other TDS, education cess is also to be deducted.

(c)There is no provision for TDS on service tax.

Further to above query, while deducting tax from payment made to Indian residents under sections 194C, 194D etc., of Income-tax Act, whether TDS should be on net amount (i.e. exclusive of service tax) or inclusive of service tax?

Section 194C(1) of the Income-tax Act provides that while paying any sum to any resident (termed as ‘contractor’) for carrying out any work, 1%/2% amount shall be deducted as income-tax at the time of credit of ‘such sum’ to account of contractor. ‘Such sum’ means amount credited to account of contractor or paid to him. This will obviously include service tax charged by contractor in his invoice, since that amount is not only credited to his account but also paid to him. Hence, TDS should be on gross amount inclusive of service tax and education cess charged by him. In case of sections 194D, 194H and 194-I, the words used are ‘credit of such income’ and not ‘credit of such sum’. Here, a view is possible that ‘income’ does not include ‘service tax’.

FAQ 40. Whether employees' contributions to provident fund, Superannuation fund etc. after the due dates are deductible?

Clause 20(b) of Form 3CD seeks the details of contributions received from employees for various funds as referred to in section 36(1)(va). There is no duty cast on the tax auditor to verify whether the amounts of PF/ESIC etc. has been correctly deducted from the employee's salary. The tax auditor's duties are limited to verify whether the amounts deducted from employees salaries have been paid over to the Govt. on or before the due date.

Section 36(1)(va) provides for deduction of any sum received by an assessee from any of his employees to which provisions of section 2(24)(x) apply, if such sum is credited by the assessee to the employee's account in the relevant fund or funds on or before the due date.

This matter has witnessed substantial litigation and the Courts have given conflicting rulings - some in favour of the employers stating that employees' share even if paid before the due date of filing of return of income can be claimed a deduction, while some rulings have held that deposit of employee's share of contribution beyond the dates prescribed under the respective legislation would not be allowed as a deduction.

The Finance Act, 2021 has put rest to this controversy by inserting an Explanation 5 to section 43B to clarify that the provisions of the said section do not apply and are deemed to never have been applied to a sum received by the assessee from any of his employees to which provisions of section 2(24)(x) applies. In other words, an employee's contribution to the specified fund would be deductible only under section 36(1)(va), if deposited in the time specified therein, and provision of section 43B would not apply in that case.

For example, employees contribution to relevant funds deducted from the salary is Rs. 1,00,000.The said amount is treated as income of the employer under section 2(24)(x).The due date for making payment of such amount to the relevant fund is, say 15thApril, 2021. If the employer does not make payment on or before the said date, the said amount would not be deductible under section 36(1)(va). It is noted that such amount would be disallowed permanently, i.e. it is not deductible in the year of payment [it was allowable prior to amendment basis some court rulings]. Accordingly, the employer needs to pay tax on such an amount, and he also needs to deposit such an amount to the relevant fund.

The payee has furnished his return of income under Section 139;

(b)

The payee has taken into account such sum for computing income;

(c)

The payee has paid the tax due on the income declared by him in such return of income; and

(d)

The payer furnishes a certificate to this effect from an accountant in Form 26A.

38. Allow payment of advance tax in a single instalment in case Section 44AE presumptive scheme is opted

Section 211 of the Income-tax Act provides the due dates and the amount of advance tax payable in instalments by the taxpayers. This provision provides that a taxpayer is required to pay the advance tax in four instalments during the financial year on the specified due dates. However, this provision allows the taxpayers who have opted for a presumptive taxation scheme under Section 44AD and Section 44ADA to pay 100% of advance tax by 15th March of the financial year.

As there are more presumptive taxation schemes allowed under Sections 44AE, 44B, 44BB, etc., this option to pay advance tax in a single instalment is allowed only for those who have opted for Section 44AD and 44ADA presumptive scheme. Where the analogy behind such a provision was to extend this option to only resident taxpayers, then this option should be allowed to those resident taxpayers as well who have opted for Section 44AE presumptive scheme. Thus, it is recommended that the option to pay the entire advance tax in a single instalment should be extended to assessees who have opted for the Section 44AE presumptive scheme.

39. Time-limit may be specified for passing an order in case of default in deduction of tax from the payment made to non-resident

As per Section 201 of the Income-tax Act, if a person responsible for the deduction of tax at source, fails to deduct the whole or any part of the tax or after deduction fails to deposit the same to the credit of the Central Government, then he shall be deemed to be an assessee-in-default.

Sub-section (3) of Section 201 provides that no order deeming a deductor to be an assessee-in-default, on failure to deduct the tax from a person resident in India, shall be passed after the expiry of 7 years from the end of the financial year in which payment is made, or credit is given or after the expiry of 2 years from the end of the financial year in which correction statement is furnished, whichever is later. However, these time limits are applicable only when TDS defaults are related to payments made to a person resident in India. In other words, sub-section (3) does not apply if there is a default in the tax deduction with respect to payments made to a non-resident.

As no time limit has been prescribed under the Act for passing an order against a person who defaults in deducting or depositing tax with respect to payments made to a non-resident, various courts have held that the department can take action in a reasonable time but what should be a reasonable time, is quite controversial.

Hence, the Government may make a necessary amendment under sub-section (3) of section 201 to specify the time limit for passing an order of assessee-in-default where a person defaults in deducting or depositing tax in respect of payments made to a non-resident. It is recommended that the Govt. should bring both provisions to par.

Consequence of failure to deduct or pay [Section 201]

8.5 Under section 201, a person is deemed to be an assessee-in-default if there is a failure to deduct tax at source or for failure to deposit the tax deducted at source after such tax has been deducted. The persons covered under the ambit of section 201 are:

(i) person referred to in section 200;

(ii) the principal officer and the company of which he is the principal officer in the cases referred to in section 194 [relating to deduction of tax at source on dividends].

Section 200(1) provides that any person deducting any tax at source in accordance with the provisions of Chapter XVII shall pay the sum so deducted to the Central Government or as the Board directs within the prescribed time. Since section 200 applies to persons deducting tax, and since it has been used in section 201, a view has been expressed that the provisions of section 201(1) do not cover failure to deduct tax at source. In order to counter this view, section 201(1) has been substituted with effect from 1-6-2002 to clarify that where a person, including the principal officer of a company,

(i) who is required to deduct any sum in accordance with the provisions of the Act; or

(ii) referred to in section 192(1A), being an employer,

does not deduct, or after so deducting fails to pay, or does not pay, the whole or any part of the tax, as required by or under the Act, he shall be deemed to an assessee in default under section 201.

A similar amendment has also been carried out in Explanation to section 191 with retrospective effect from 1-6-2003.

Dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates [Sections 203 & 206C]

8.6 An assessee is entitled to credit in respect of tax deducted at source (‘TDS’) and tax collected at source (‘TCS’) on the basis of a certificate issued by the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source. Such certificate has to be enclosed with the return of income to claim the credit.

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 proposed dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates and, inter alia1, provided that on and after 1-4-2005:

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source should file quarterly statements with the income-tax authority or authorised person;

◆ such authority or person would furnish a statement of tax deducted or collected at source (‘the Statement’) to the payee or buyer;

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source need not furnish certificate to the payee or buyer; and

◆ the payee or buyer would be entitled to the credit for TDS or TCS based on the statement furnished by such authority or person.

The Finance Act, 2005 postponed the implementation of the above by a year and the Finance Act, 2006 further postponed it up to 31-3-2008.

◆ Section 203(3) of the Act providing that a payer need not issue a certificate of TDS;

Credit allowed only if relevant income is taxable - A tax credit can be given only in cases where the tax is paid on the income in respect of which deduction has been made at source [CIT v. Tanjore Permanent Bank Ltd. [1987] 30 Taxman 265 (Mad.)].

Payment to Central Government is necessary - Mere deduction of tax at source will not entitle one to credit for tax deducted if person responsible for deduction at source has not made it over to Central Government [Asstt. CIT v. Om Prakash Gattani [2001] 117 Taxman 549 (Gau.)].

Since what was deducted by the Director of Lotteries was Sikkim income-tax and not income-tax u/s 194B and further, amount so deducted had not been paid to Central Government, thus, assessee was not entitled to any credit of tax based on certificate issued by the Director of Lotteries [M. K. Raghu v. Asstt. CIT [2009] 182 Taxman 362 (Ker.)].

However, in Kartik Vijaysinh Sonavane v. DCIT [2021] 132 taxmann.com 293/[2022] 284 Taxman 278 (Guj.), it has been held that where TDS has been deducted by employer of assessee, it will always been open for department to recover same from said employer and credit of same could not have been denied to assessee.

Deduction of excess amount - If it is found that excess amounts have been deducted from the payments made to the assessee, which are in excess of his tax liability, then the excess amount of tax collected from such assessee shall be refunded to him [K. S. Venugopalan, Operator, Travancore Cochin Chemicals Ltd. v. ITO [2015] 54 taxmann.com 248/229 Taxman 222 (Ker.)].

In case of bonds - In relation to interest on deep discount bonds, any deduction made of tax at source and paid to Central Government is required to be treated as payment of tax on behalf of owner of security or unit holder [CIT v. Smt. Sonal Bansal [2008] 167 Taxman 311 (P&H)].

In case of co-owners/joint owners - In case of two sharing parties, credit for tax deduction at source is to be assigned to each of such persons deriving income from common investment, i.e., in same proportion in which they share income [CIT v. Punjab Financial Corporation [2009] 181 Taxman 209 (P&H)].

Where assessee, co-owner of a property, paid share of rental income to other co-owners without deducting TDS from rent received from tenant and no TDS credit was claimed by other co-owners, assessee would be entitled to credit of tax deducted at source in its entirety [CIT v. Ganesh Narayan Brijlal Ltd. [2016] 74 taxmann.com 96/244 Taxman 14 (Cal.)].

In case of deceased person – Where assessee offered interest income received on account of her deceased husband in her return of income and tax paid also reflected in Form 26AS, corresponding TDS was to be allowed to assessee [Nayana Kanakbhai Hutheesing v. ITO [2023] 150 taxmann.com 182/292 Taxman 588 (Guj.)].

In case of joint venture - Where TDS certificates were issued in name of joint venture for executing a works contract, in view of the failure of the joint venture to file return and claim credit for TDS certificates, said credit could be allowed to assessee in capacity of individual co-joint venturer [CIT v. Bhooratnam & Co. [2013] 29 taxmann.com 275/216 Taxman 6 (AP)].

Inadvertent mistake - Where, due to an inadvertent mistake of vendor, TDS related to assessee's sister concern was credited to assessee's TDS account, assessee could claim credit of such TDS, provided its sister concern had not availed benefit of such TDS certificates [CIT v. Relcom [2015] 62 taxmann.com 190/234 Taxman 693 (Delhi)].

Incorrect details - In case deductor failed to upload correct details in Form 26A, benefit of TDS should be given to assessee on basis of evidence produced before Department [PCIT v. Tata Communications Ltd. [2019] 111 taxmann.com 259/267 Taxman 497 (SC)].

Dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates [Sections 203 & 206C]

8.6 An assessee is entitled to credit in respect of tax deducted at source (‘TDS’) and tax collected at source (‘TCS’) on the basis of a certificate issued by the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source. Such certificate has to be enclosed with the return of income to claim the credit.

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 proposed dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates and, inter alia1, provided that on and after 1-4-2005:

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source should file quarterly statements with the income-tax authority or authorised person;

◆ such authority or person would furnish a statement of tax deducted or collected at source (‘the Statement’) to the payee or buyer;

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source need not furnish certificate to the payee or buyer; and

◆ the payee or buyer would be entitled to the credit for TDS or TCS based on the statement furnished by such authority or person.

The Finance Act, 2005 postponed the implementation of the above by a year and the Finance Act, 2006 further postponed it up to 31-3-2008.

8.6-1 Analysis of amendments - The effect of the above amendments is as follows:

◆ the credit for TDS or TCS, in respect of the financial years 2008-09 and 2009-10 (assessment years 2009-10 and 2010-11) will be available on the basis of certificates issued by the payer or the person responsible for collecting tax at source; and

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source will have to continue to issue certificates to the payee or the buyer, in respect of the tax deducted or collected at source during the financial years 2008-09 and 2009-10.

Similarly, the second proviso of section 206C(5) provides that the prescribed authority shall furnish such statement of TCS. Mandatory and automatic - The interest is to compensate the revenue for the loss which it has suffered on account of late receipt of the tax. Thus, provisions of interest u/s 201 are mandatory and automatic and interest has to be paid from date on which tax was deductible till date on which tax is actually paid [CIT v. Rathi Gum Industries [1995] 213 ITR 98 (Raj.)].

Even if assessee was bona fide in not making such deduction, it was liable to pay interest [Sun Outsourcing Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2018] 92 taxmann.com 339 (AP)].

Interest u/s 201(1A) is leviable even where recipient is a loss-making company [CIT v. Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board [2011] 14 taxmann.com 73/202 Taxman 454 (Mad.)]. Also see, CIT v. Punjab Infrastructure Dev. Board [2016] 76 taxmann.com 365/[2017] 245 Taxman 183 (P&H), SLP granted inPunjab Infrastructure Dev Board v. GENERAL

Constitutional validity - Section 201 is a penal provision to treat a person as an assessee-in-default if there is a failure to deduct the tax or to pay the tax after it is deducted. Sufficient safeguards have been provided in the section itself, and as such it cannot be considered that the provisions are ultra vires the Constitution [Mittal Steel Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [1999] 240 ITR 707 (Kar.)].

ASSESSEE-IN-DEFAULT

Competent authority - In terms of section 201, it is assessing authority who is competent person to pass an order holding an assessee to be 'assessee-in-default' and not Director General (Systems) [CIT v. Kingfisher Airlines Ltd. [2014] 49 taxmann.com 49 (Kar.)].

AO couldn't treat payer as assessee-in-default without examining his submission justifying non-deduction of tax [Remco (BHEL) House Building Co-Operative Society Ltd. v. ITO [2015] 58 taxmann.com 317/232 Taxman 355 (Kar.)].

AO has jurisdiction to demand amount of tax not deducted at source by an order passed u/s 201(1) and 201(1A). If assessee takes defence that payee has paid tax on money, it is for him to prove it; AO is not obliged to explore possible defences and to collect evidence in support thereof [Nopany Marketing Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 57 taxmann.com 186/231 Taxman 802 (Cal.)].

No demand notice required - By virtue of provisions u/s 201, a person is deemed to be an 'assessee-in-default' in view of statutory provision contained therein and in such a case, there is no scope of giving further notice of demand u/s 156 which is applicable only in cases when any tax, interest, penalty, fine or any other sum is payable in consequence of any order passed under the 1961 Act. Thus, in a case where section 201(1) is attracted there is no need of giving any notice u/s 156 and if any such notice is given the same should be held to be redundant [PILCOM v. CIT [2011] 11 taxmann.com 103 (Cal.)].

Section 191 vis-à-vis section 201 - The language of the Explanation to section 191 and section 201(1) is almost similar except with one difference. In the former section, the deductor shall be deemed to be an assessee-in-default where the assessee has also failed to pay such tax directly, whereas in section 201(1), this condition is not mentioned. While interpreting the provisions of sections 191 and 201(1), a harmonious construction has to be adopted and such interpretation is to be put which gives meaning and purpose to both the provisions. Explanation to section 191 specifically mentions "....be deemed to be an assessee in default within the meaning of section 201(1) in respect of such tax". The above meaning, thus, has to be read in section 201(1), which has been specifically provided for. Not repeating the said condition again in section 201(1) is inconsequential. Thus, the deductor who fails to deduct TDS shall be deemed to be an assessee-in-default only when the assessee has also failed to pay such tax directly. Thus, it flows that there is no occasion to treat the deductor as an assessee-in-default unless the assessee has not paid the tax directly [Jagran Prakashan Ltd. v. DCIT [2012] 21 taxmann.com 489/209 Taxman 92 (All.)].

Assessee not in default - There is nothing in section 201 to treat the employer as the defaulter where there is a shortfall in the deduction of tax at source. The expression 'as required by or under the Act' grammatically refers only to the duty to pay the tax that is deducted and cannot refer to the duty to deduct the tax. If there is any shortfall due to any difference of opinion as to the taxability of any item, the employer cannot be declared to be an assessee-in-default [P. V. Rajagopal v. UOI [1998] 99 Taxman 475 (AP)]. Also see, CIT v. Sony India (P.) Ltd. [2012] 17 taxmann.com 126/210 Taxman 55 (Kar.).

Section 201 of the Act provides that where any person including principal officer of a company required to deduct any tax, (hereinafter collectively referred as 'person responsible') does not deduct or does not pay or after deducting fails to pay, the whole or any part of the tax, he is deemed to be 'an assessee in default in respect of such tax' (hereafter referred as 'Assessee in default').

The Supreme Court in Hindustan Coca Cola Beverage (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2007] 163 Taxman 355/ 293 ITR 226 upheld the decision of Tribunal that if the tax is paid by the payee, the shortfall in deduction of tax cannot be reco-vered from the payer or the deductor.

11.8.1 Amendment

Finance Act, 2012 inserts first proviso in sub-section (1), with effect from 1-7-2012 to provide that in certain circumstances person responsible shall not be deemed to be assessee in default.

Person responsible, not to be regarded as assessee in default would be person responsible who fails to deduct the whole or any part of tax in accordance with the provisions of Chapter XVII-B from the amount cre-dited or paid to a resident, subject to fulfilment of the conditions.

11.8.2 Conditions

To enable person responsible to claim that he shall not be assessee in default, the following conditions need to be complied:

(a) The payee is a resident.

(b) The resident payee has furnished his return of income under section 139.

Where a payee does not furnish his return of income, benefit of the first proviso would not be available to person responsible.

Return must be furnished under section 139 implying that any delayed or revised return would satisfy the condition. Any return other than under section 139 is not covered.

(c) The resident payee has included the amount paid or credited (without suffering TDS) for computing income in the return.

(d) The resident payee has paid the tax on income declared in the return furnished.

(e) Person responsible must furnish a certificate to this effect from an accountant in prescribed form.

The prescribed form would contain the details to be furnished. The details could be in relation to the conditions imposed, namely: furnishing of return; inclusion of the amount credited or paid on which tax is not deducted in the income returned; and tax is paid on such income.

An Explanation is inserted after section 201(4) to define 'accountant', having the same meaning as assigned to it in Explanation below section 288(2).

11.8.3 Analysis

11.8.3a Non-application of proviso

(a) Sub-section (1) deems person responsible as assessee in default, inter alia, in case of non-payment also. However, the proviso restricts its applicability to person responsible who has failed to deduct tax.

(b) It applies only in case of a payment to a resident. Accordingly, when payment or credit is made to a non-resident the proviso would not apply. In other words, in such a case, person responsible would be deemed to be assessee in default, as the first proviso will not apply.

11.8.3b Certificate - On reading the provision, it creates an impression that person responsible has to obtain and furnish certificate from accountant. However, since the details pertain to a resident payee, it appears that the resident payee will have to obtain the certificate and provide the same to person responsible to enable him to claim that he may not be consi-dered as assessee in default. However, a specific obligation is not cast on the resident payee. In absence thereof, Person responsible may have difficulties in obtaining and furnishing such certificate.

11.8.3c If payee is not required to file a return of income - In such a case, obviously, the conditions stipulated cannot be fulfilled. Hence, person responsible will not be able to comply with the requirement of furnishing certificate from accountant. In such a case, on a plain reading, and person the proviso would not apply responsible can be treated as assessee in default and all the consequences would follow.

An Explanation has now been inserted in the said section with effect from 1-6-2003 to clarify that if whole or part of the tax has not been deducted, and such tax has not been paid by the assessee direct, then without prejudice to other consequences, the person who has not deducted tax (including the principal officer of a company in case of dividend payments) shall be deemed to be an assessee in default as referred to in section 201(1) of the Act in respect of such tax.

The Memorandum explaining the provisions of the Finance Bill states that “the Bill proposes to clarify that if a person does not deduct the whole or any part of tax, he shall be deemed to be an assessee in default as referred to in sub-section (1) of section 201 in respect of such tax unless such income-tax has been paid by the assessee himself.”

Courts have taken a view that if tax on such income has already been paid by the payee, then tax cannot be recovered again from the payer. This position is also clarified in the Circular issued by the CBDT in F. No. 275/201/95-IT(B), dated 29-1-1997 [cited in Cresent Housing (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2002] 75 TTJ (Mad.) 57] as follows :

However, the Tribunal in its decision in Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. ITO TDS[2000] 68 TTJ (Mum.) 220 had gone a step further and held that in view of section 191, the tax which is not deducted under Chapter XVII cannot be recovered whether or not the payer has paid the tax and tax has to be recovered from the payee (assessee) direct. It appears that the amendment gives legislative approval to the CBDT clarification and neutralizes the aforesaid decision of Mumbai Tribunal.

However, the Explanation provides that mere non-deduction of tax will not deem the payer to be an assessee in default. ◆ Section 201(1) provides that if the payer deducts tax at source but does not pay such tax, he is deemed to be an assessee in default. This situation is not covered by the Explanation, which deals only with the situation where the payer does not deduct the required tax at source.

8.4-4 The Statement - Note the following :

There is no requirement about furnishing a copy of the Statement to the Assessing Officer of the payee/buyer.

◆ The Statement, in respect of TDS, should specify the amount of tax deducted or paid [under section 192(1A)] and other particulars as may be prescribed. Thus, the Statement would contain details of the tax deducted as per the provisions of the Chapter and paid under section 192(1A).

◆ The Statement, in respect of TCS, should specify the amount of tax collected.

◆ Thus, it may be noted that the Statement must specify:

■ TDS Statement:

● Amount of tax deducted as per the provisions of the Chapter; and/or

● Amount of tax paid under section 192(1A); and/or

● Such other particulars as may be prescribed.

■ TCS Statement:

● Amount of tax collected; and/or

● Such other particulars as may be prescribed.

8.4-5 Credit for the tax deducted or collected - The provision in relation to :—

◆ TDS [section 199(3)], reads as follows: “where any deduction is made. . . on or after the 1st day of April, 2005 and paid to the Central Government, the amount of tax deducted and specified in the statement referred to in section 203AA shall be treated as tax paid on behalf of the person referred to in sub-section (1) . . . and credit shall be given to him for the amount so deducted in the assessment... without production of certificate.” (Emphasis supplied)

◆ TCS [first proviso to section 206C(4)] reads: “provided that where any amount is collected... on or after 1st day of April, 2005 and paid... to the credit of the Central Government, the amount of tax collected and specified in statement referred to... shall be deemed as payment of tax on behalf of the person from whom the amount has been collected and credit shall be given to him for the amount so collected in the assessment... without production of certificate.” (Emphasis supplied)

Thus, the amount of tax deducted/collected and specified in the Statement would be treated as tax paid on behalf of the payee/buyer. It appears, the payee/buyer would get credit for such tax deducted/collected on his/her behalf. For whatever reasons, the amount of tax deducted/collected is not specified in the Statement, the amount not specified would not be treated as tax deducted/collected on behalf of the payee/buyer and credit will not be available for the same to the payee/buyer.

In this connection an issue may arise about the treatment of tax deducted or collected and specified in the statement but not paid by the payer/collector. If appears that to the extent tax deducted/collected, whether specified in the statement or not the recovery cannot be enforced against the payee/buyer, for the following reasons :

(i) Section 203AA and second proviso to section 206C(5), respectively provide that the prescribed income-tax authorities or authorised person shall prepare and collect the statement of tax deducted/paid [under section 192(1A)] on tax collected.

(ii) Section 199(3) and first proviso to section 206C(4) treat the tax deducted or collected and specified in the statement as tax paid on behalf of the payee or buyer. Thus, the tax deducted on collected, whether paid or not is the relevant amount which can be considered as paid on behalf of the payee/buyer.

(iii) Section 205 of the Act provides that where the tax is deductible at source under applicable provisions of Chapter XVII, the assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income.

(iv) Section 191 contemplates direct payment by the payee only in a case where tax is deducted in terms of Chapter XVII and not in a case where the tax is deducted and not paid.

While claiming the credit, the payee or the buyer may face some difficulties on account of one or more of the following illustrative situations :

◆ The Statement is not received from the prescribed income-tax authority or authorised agency in time. In that case, his return of income would be delayed, with attendant consequences. Alternatively, he may not be able to claim credit for the same.

Section 203

Finance Act, 2008

Dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates [Sections 203 & 206C]

8.6 An assessee is entitled to credit in respect of tax deducted at source ('TDS') and tax collected at source ('TCS') on the basis of a certificate issued by the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source. Such certificate has to be enclosed with the return of income to claim the credit.

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 proposed dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates and, inter alia1, provided that on and after 1-4-2005:

the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source should file quarterly statements with the income-tax authority or authorised person;

such authority or person would furnish a statement of tax deducted or collected at source ('the Statement') to the payee or buyer;

the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source need not furnish certificate to the payee or buyer; and

the payee or buyer would be entitled to the credit for TDS or TCS based on the statement furnished by such authority or person.

The Finance Act, 2005 postponed the implementation of the above by a year and the Finance Act, 2006 further postponed it up to 31-3-2008.

Pending stabilisation of the system, the Finance Act, 2008 has amended with effect from 1-4-2008, the following provisions to provide that the amendments made therein by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004, as further amended by the Finance Act, 2005 and Finance Act, 2006 would become effective from 1-4-2010 instead of 1-4-2008 as provided heretobefore:

Section 203(3) of the Act providing that a payer need not issue a certificate of TDS;

First proviso to section 206C(5) providing that a person responsible for collecting tax at source need not issue a certificate of TCS.

Further, the Explanation below section 139(9) providing that if the proof of tax deducted or collected at source is not attached on or after 1-4-2008, the return would not be considered as defective has been amended by deleting the words 'on or after 1st April, 2008'.

8.6-1 Analysis of amendments - The effect of the above amendments is as follows:

the credit for TDS or TCS, in respect of the financial years 2008-09 and 2009-10 (assessment years 2009-10 and 2010-11) will be available on the basis of certificates issued by the payer or the person responsible for collecting tax at source; and

the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source will have to continue to issue certificates to the payee or the buyer, in respect of the tax deducted or collected at source during the financial years 2008-09 and 2009-10.

Section 203AA of the Act provides that the prescribed authority shall furnish the statement of TDS in the prescribed form and specifying prescribed particulars. Similarly, the second proviso of section 206C(5) provides that the prescribed authority shall furnish such statement of TCS. The Finance Act, 2006 had postponed the applicability of these provisions to the financial year beginning on or after 1-4-2008. Now, no amendment has been made to these provisions by the Finance Act, 2008.

TCS [first proviso to section 206C(4)] reads: "provided that where any amount is collected... on or after 1st day of April, 2005 and paid... to the credit of the Central Government, the amount of tax collected and specified in statement referred to... shall be deemed as payment of tax on behalf of the person from whom the amount has been collected and credit shall be given to him for the amount so collected in the assessment... without production of certificate." (Emphasis supplied)

Thus, the amount of tax deducted/collected and specified in the Statement would be treated as tax paid on behalf of the payee/buyer. It appears, the payee/buyer would get credit for such tax deducted/collected on his/her behalf. For whatever reasons, the amount of tax deducted/collected is not specified in the Statement, the amount not specified would not be treated as tax deducted/collected on behalf of the payee/buyer and credit will not be available for the same to the payee/buyer.

In this connection an issue may arise about the treatment of tax deducted or collected and specified in the statement but not paid by the payer/collector. If appears that to the extent tax deducted/collected, whether specified in the statement or not the recovery cannot be enforced against the payee/buyer, for the following reasons :

(i)

Section 203AA and second proviso to section 206C(5), respectively provide that the prescribed income-tax authorities or authorised person shall prepare and collect the statement of tax deducted/paid [under section 192(1A)] on tax collected.

(ii)

Section 199(3) and first proviso to section 206C(4) treat the tax deducted or collected and specified in the statement as tax paid on behalf of the payee or buyer. Thus, the tax deducted on collected, whether paid or not is the relevant amount which can be considered as paid on behalf of the payee/buyer.

(ii)

Section 205 of the Act provides that where the tax is deductible at source under applicable provisions of Chapter XVII, the assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income;

(iii)

Section 191 contemplates direct payment by the payee only in a case where tax is deducted in terms of Chapter XVII and not in a case where the tax is deducted and not paid.

Finance Act, 2008

Dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates [Sections 203 & 206C]

8.6 An assessee is entitled to credit in respect of tax deducted at source ('TDS') and tax collected at source ('TCS') on the basis of a certificate issued by the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source. Such certificate has to be enclosed with the return of income to claim the credit.

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 proposed dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates and, inter alia1, provided that on and after 1-4-2005:

the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source should file quarterly statements with the income-tax authority or authorised person;

such authority or person would furnish a statement of tax deducted or collected at source ('the Statement') to the payee or buyer;

the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source need not furnish certificate to the payee or buyer; and

the payee or buyer would be entitled to the credit for TDS or TCS based on the statement furnished by such authority or person.

The Finance Act, 2005 postponed the implementation of the above by a year and the Finance Act, 2006 further postponed it up to 31-3-2008.

Pending stabilisation of the system, the Finance Act, 2008 has amended with effect from 1-4-2008, the following provisions to provide that the amendments made therein by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004, as further amended by the Finance Act, 2005 and Finance Act, 2006 would become effective from 1-4-2010 instead of 1-4-2008 as provided heretobefore:

Section 203(3) of the Act providing that a payer need not issue a certificate of TDS;

First proviso to section 206C(5) providing that a person responsible for collecting tax at source need not issue a certificate of TCS.

Further, the Explanation below section 139(9) providing that if the proof of tax deducted or collected at source is not attached on or after 1-4-2008, the return would not be considered as defective has been amended by deleting the words 'on or after 1st April, 2008'.

8.6-1 Analysis of amendments - The effect of the above amendments is as follows:

the credit for TDS or TCS, in respect of the financial years 2008-09 and 2009-10 (assessment years 2009-10 and 2010-11) will be available on the basis of certificates issued by the payer or the person responsible for collecting tax at source; and

the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source will have to continue to issue certificates to the payee or the buyer, in respect of the tax deducted or collected at source during the financial years 2008-09 and 2009-10.

Section 203AA of the Act provides that the prescribed authority shall furnish the statement of TDS in the prescribed form and specifying prescribed particulars. Similarly, the second proviso of section 206C(5) provides that the prescribed authority shall furnish such statement of TCS. The Finance Act, 2006 had postponed the applicability of these provisions to the financial year beginning on or after 1-4-2008. Now, no amendment has been made to these provisions by the Finance Act, 2008.

4.6.3b Past Position - The amendment is effective from and applies to assessment year 2013-14 and thereafter. In that case, the question arises what could be the date of allowance of the expenditure, in similar circumstances, in respect of any assessment year prior to assessment year 2013-14?

Effectively, the amendment cures a defect or removes an anomaly. Hence, it should be considered as retrospective, for the following reasons: 1. While explaining the reasons for the amendments in section 201 and section 40(a)(ia), the Memorandum, inter alia, notes as follows :

"... Section 191 of the Act provides that a person shall be deemed to be assessee in default in respect of non/short deduction of tax only in cases where the payee has also failed to pay the tax directly. Therefore, the deductor cannot be treated as assessee in default in respect of non/short deduction of tax if the payee has discharged his tax liability.

The payer is liable to pay interest under section 201(1A) on the amount of non/short deduction of tax from the date on which such tax was deductible to the date on which the payee has discharged his tax liability directly. As there is no one-to-one correlation between the tax to be deducted by the payer and the tax paid by the payee, there is lack of clarity as to when it can be said that payer has paid the taxes directly. Also, there is no clarity on the issue of the cut-off date, i.e. the date on which it can be said that the payee has discharged his tax liability.

In order to provide clarity regarding discharge of tax liability ... it is proposed to amend section 201...

A related issue to the above is the disallowance under section 40(a)(ia) of certain business expenditure ...

In order to rationalise the provisions of disallowance ... it is proposed to amend section 40(a)(ia) ...

These beneficial provisions are supposed to be applicable only in the case of resident payee".

2. CBDT by Circular No 275/201/95-IT (B), dated 29-1-1997 clarified that "no demand visualized under section 201(1) of the Income-tax Act should be enforced after the tax deductor has satisfied the officer- in-charge of TDS, that taxes due have been paid by the deductee-assessee. However, this will not alter the liability to charge interest ...".

3. Supreme Court in Hindustan Coca Cola Beverage (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2007] 163 Taxman 355/ 293 ITR 226, applying the above circular, accepted the contention that the tax cannot be recovered from the assessee.

4. Having regard to the above position in law, the tax could not have been recovered and accordingly, as such, the question of any payment by the deductor would not arise. In that case, the deductor would not be in a position to claim the expenditure as allowable, since they would not be in a position to fulfil the condition stipulated by section 40(a)(ia) of the Act. In other words, the deductor would suffer the loss, although, the tax is paid directly by the deductee. Obviously, this cannot be a position in law.

5. To remove the anomaly and/or hardships to the deductor, as explained in the Memorandum, the position in law is now clarified. For the purpose, certain procedural requirement is also introduced in the form of furnishing of a certificate from Accountant, as detailed above.

6. Thus, the amendment removes the defect and, hence, as held by Supreme Court in CIT v. Alom Extrusions Ltd. [2009] 185 Taxman 416/ 319 ITR 306 [following its earlier decisions in Allied Motors (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 91 Taxman 205/ 224 ITR 677 (SC) and CIT v. J.H. Gotla [1985] 23 Taxman 14J/ 156 ITR 323 (SC)], wherein it was observed (from headnotes) :

"When a proviso in a section is inserted to remedy unintended consequences and to make the section workable, the proviso which supplies an obvious omission therein is required to be read retrospectively in operation, particularly to give effect to the section as a whole. ... If strict construction leads to a result not intended to be subserved by the object of the legislation, and if another construction is possible apart from the literal construction, then that construction should be preferred".

While claiming the credit, the payee or the buyer may face some difficulties on account of one or more of the following illustrative situations :

◆ The Statement is not received from the prescribed income-tax authority or authorised agency in time. In that case, his return of income would be delayed, with attendant consequences. Alternatively, he may not be able to claim credit for the same. ◆ The Statement may not give complete particulars of the tax deducted at source or collected at source from the payee or the buyer. In that case, it is not clear who can be approached? The prescribed authority or the authorised agency or the payer or the collector? Under the old Scheme of credit he could approach the payer/collector. Further, in absence of any communication from the payer, it may be difficult for him to show and establish that the tax has been deducted or collected or paid.

◆ The Statement may contain certain mistakes or information, which is not accurate. There is no provision for rectification of the Statement by the prescribed income-tax authority or the authorised agency.

◆ In case of the receipt of the Statement subsequent to the filing of return, there is no clarity about the mode and manner in which the credit can be claimed.

◆ The scheme, as per the amendments, does not provide for any consequences in case where the prescribed authority or the authorised agency does not furnish the Statement of tax deducted/collected to the payee/buyer. Further, in case of a failure to furnish the Statement by the prescribed authority or the authorised agency, there is no clarity about the remedies available to the payee/buyer.

Common number for TDS and TCS

8.5 Presently :

◆ Section 203A obliges a person responsible for deduction of tax (‘the payer’) to obtain a tax deduction account number (‘TAN’); and

◆ Section 206CA obliges a person responsible for collection of tax (‘the collector’) to obtain a tax collection account number (‘TCN’).

Further, section 272BB provides for penalty for failure to comply with the provisions of section 203A of Rs. 10,000; and section 272BBB provides for penalty for failure to comply with the provisions of section 206CA of Rs. 10,000.

To simplify and rationalise the procedure, the amendments provide for a common TDS and TCS number and for the purpose the following amendments have been carried out :

◆ Section 203A is substituted to provide for the common number;

◆ Section 206CA is made inoperative from 1-10-2004;

◆ Section 272BBB is made inoperative from 1-10-2004, since section 272BBB levies penalty for non-compliance with section 203A.

All the amendments are effective from 1-10-2004.

The substituted section 203A provides as follows :

◆ The payer or the collector, deducting or collecting tax, who has not been allotted either a TAN or TCN shall apply to the Assessing Officer for the allotment of a tax deduction and collection account number (‘TDCN’);

◆ Such person shall quote either TAN or TCN or TDCN in :

■ all challans for payment of tax collected or deducted [see section 200/206C(3)];

■ all certificates furnished for tax deducted or tax collected [see section 203/206C(5)];

■ all the returns required to be filed under sections 206 and/or 206C(5A)/(5B); and

■ other documents relating to such transactions, as may be prescribed in the interests of the revenue.

It appears that, effectively :

◆ The payer or the collector, who is allotted TAN and/or TCN have to continue with the existing account numbers and quote them in the requisite documents;

◆ In case of the payer who has been allotted TAN and becomes liable to collect tax at source after 1-10-2004, he will have to apply for TDCN;

◆ In case of the collector who has been allotted TCS and becomes liable to deduct tax at source after 1-10-2004, he will have to apply for TDCN; and

◆ In case of any person, who has not been allotted either TDS or TCS and becomes liable either to deduct or collect tax at source after 1-10-2004, he will have to apply for TDCN.

Filing of TDS returns [Section 206]

8.6 Presently :

◆ the TDS return is required to be filed with prescribed income-tax authority; and

◆ any person, other than a company, can file paper/electronic returns [section 206(1) and (2)].

In case of companies it is mandatory to file the returns on computer media [proviso below section 206(2)].

8.6-1 Amendments made - An amendment in section 206(1) provides that the returns can also be filed with such other authority or agency as may be prescribed.

case_summary.text: Assessee entitled to TDS credit even if employer fails to deposit TDS; recovery to be made from employer:ITAT

INCOME TAX: Where employee claimed TDS credit on salary, but employer failed to deposit deducted TDS with government, employee was still entitled to TDS credit in view of sections 201 and 205, which bar direct demand on employee, and recovery could only be effected from employer, not from employee.

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section  205,  read with sections  199  and  201, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  401,  read with sections  390  and  398  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Deduction of tax at source -  Bar against direct demand on assessee (Salary)  - Assessee-employee filed return of income claiming credit of tax deducted at source (TDS) on salary - Return was processed under section 143(1) allowing partial TDS credit - Assessee contended that employer had deducted TDS on entire salary and credit should be allowed - Revenue contended that employer had not deposited deducted TDS in Government account and, therefore, credit could not be allowed - Whether in view of provisions of sections 201 and 205, which make employer who failed to remit tax deducted at source, person in default, and employee could not be called upon to pay such tax again, assessee was entitled to credit of TDS and recovery could be effected from employer but not from assessee - Held, yes [Paras 6.1 and 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee–employee filed a return declaring total income of about Rs. 70.37 lakhs for the year under consideration and claimed TDS credit of about Rs. 18.10 lakhs.

■

The return was processed under section 143(1) by CPC, which allowed TDS credit of about Rs. 0.60 lakhs only, restricting the balance claim.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the AO to grant an opportunity of being heard, verify the TDS with Form 26AS and other relevant material to ascertain whether it related to the income offered in the year, and thereafter grant credit if the claim was found correct.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee contended that his employer had paid salary of about Rs. 57.50 lakhs and deducted TDS of about Rs. 17.50 lakhs for which credit should be allowed; the Revenue contended the employer had not deposited the deducted TDS in the Government account and, therefore, credit could not be allowed.

HELD: ■

It is observed that the Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Aditya Deepak Nasta v. ITO (IT Appeal Nos. 3293/M/2024, dated 20.09.2024) has also dealt with an identical issue/situation, wherein though the employer had deducted the TDS but not deposited in the Government account and therefore benefit of TDS was denied to the assessee. The Co-ordinate Bench while analyzing the relevant provisions of law and the identical issue as involved in the instant case, ultimately granted relief to the assessee, and held that: "From the provisions of section 201, where an employer does not deduct or, after deducting, fails to pay the tax, such person is deemed to be an assessee in default. Under section 205, where tax is deductible at source, the assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax himself to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income. In cumulative effect, sections 201 and 205 make the employer, who failed to remit tax deducted at source, the person in default, and the employee cannot be called upon to pay such tax again. In Yashpal Sahni v. ACIT (2007) 293 ITR 539 (Bom), it was held that failure to issue Form 16 or deposit TDS does not shift liability from the employer to the employee, and the Revenue cannot recover the amount once again from the assessee. In Kartik Vijaysinh Sonavane v. DCIT 440 ITR 11 (Guj), it was held that the Department is precluded from denying the benefit of tax deducted at source by the employer and credit shall be given to the assessee. On the aforesaid analyzations, the assessee cannot be treated as assessee in default as per section 199 and recovery can be effected from the employer but not from the assessee. Consequently, the Assessing Officer was directed to grant the credit of TDS and re-compute the income accordingly." [Para 6.1]

■

that the Department is precluded from denying the benefit of tax deducted at source by the employer and credit shall be given to the assessee. On the aforesaid analyzations, the assessee cannot be treated as assessee in default as per section 199 and recovery can be effected from the employer but not from the assessee. Consequently, the Assessing Officer was directed to grant the credit of TDS and re-compute the income accordingly." [Para 6.1]

■ As the issue is covered in favour of the Assessee by the aforesaid decision, hence on the same footing/direction the Assessee is entitled to get the benefit of the TDS deducted by his employer but not deposited in Government account. Thus, the AO is directed to grant the credit of TDS and re-compute the income of the Assessee accordingly. It is clarified that the Department is always at liberty and empowered to take appropriate action against the employer for recovery of TDS deducted, but not against the employee, for recovery of TDS amount deducted but not deposited by the employer, as per the provisions of law, as applicable. [Para 7]

■

In the result, the appeal filed by the Assessee stands allowed. [Para 8]
